title: Cognitive Bias
body:
**Cognitive bias** covers systematic errors in reasoning that affect users, designers and
researchers alike. They are systematic, so more data collected the same way does not average
them out.

```
pattern matching       finding structure in noise, which is what makes people
                       see trends in random price movements
confirmation bias      weighting evidence that supports a held position more
                       heavily than evidence against it
availability bias      judging frequency by how easily an example comes to mind,
                       so widely reported events feel more common than they are
anchoring              the first number offered shapes every later judgement
```

The course connects these to the statistical errors in [[STATISTICS]]. A false positive is a
Type I error and a false negative is a Type II error, and any system tuned to reduce one
produces more of the other, which [[Type I and Type II Errors]] states
formally. That trade becomes an ethical decision as soon as the two errors fall on different
people: a fraud detection system tuned to catch more fraud freezes more legitimate accounts.

Researcher bias is the same failure inside the process that evaluates a system. A test designed
by the people who built the thing, on data they chose, measures what they expected to find,
which is why [[Usability Testing]] in [[HUMAN COMPUTER INTERACTION]] insists on
observing users who were not involved in the design.
